power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: There is however reason to believe that mediation analysis is not always conducted in a completely a priori manner, which has serious consequences for the validity of the reported has only been used to examine mediation analyses. It was developed to evaluate evidential value from sets of statistical tests which primarily use confidence intervals (rather than p-values), and this measure requires additional validation, which we provide in Study 1. Study 1 uses a Monte Carlo simulation study to demonstrate how flexibility in mediation analysis can manifest in false-positive rates far greater than the nominal 𝛼𝛼 level and this inflated false-positive rate is reflected accurately by the RP index. Study 2 compares the distribution of published mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology with simulations of mediation analyses at different levels of statistical power. Our results indicate that mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology research are typically underpowered and/or show signs of selective reporting, which substantially limits the evidential value of the literature. We conclude by discussing ways to improve the evidential value of mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology research.

We ran a series of simulations to determine how the RP scores ought to be distributed for simple mediation analyses when adequately powered (80-95% power), low-powered (33-79% power), and null effects (~5% false-positive rate). We used the simstudy::genCorData R function (Goldfield & Wjciak-Jens, 2019) to create each simulated dataset with pre-specified population-level correlations among the three variables (X, the independent variable; M, the mediator, and Y, the outcome variable). To test the simulated indirect effects, we used the mediate function from the psych package for R (Revelle, 2015) with default options (alpha = .05; 5,000 bootstraps; percentile CIs). We verified that this tool gives results consistent with the PROCESS macro (Hayes, 2022). Just like with the test statistics collected from marketing and consumer psychology journals, RP scores were calculated using Equation 1.

All simulations were designed such that the RP > 0 peak of their respective RP distributions matched the peak of the marketing and consumer psychology journals' RP distribution. 5 This allowed us to compare the shapes of the simulated and observed distributions directly using absolute frequencies. In our final simulated distributions, mediation analyses reached statistical significance in 87% (a<b), 89% (a=b), and 89% (a > b) of tests designed to simulate adequate power, 58% (a<b), 60% (a=b), and 60% (a > b) of tests simulating low power.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 242 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: R history (2), RStudio session files (240). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

-  We classified 90 files: 20 data, 46 code, 4 documentation, 10 materials, 10 unknown.
-  We found 20 tabular data files and extracted 260 columns from 12 of them.
-  We grouped the files into 2 study groups (ex1, ex2), plus 4 collection-level files (README/ro-crate metadata).

table.sample_values: A oneway ANOVA revealed that participants experienced greater physical discomfort when they maintained a standing posture (Mstanding = 2.26 vs. Msitting = 1.62; F(1, 109) = 8.12, p < .01, n2 = .07). | Consistent with our expectation, participants in the resource scarcity condition also reported a higher promotion orientation (M = 7.21, SD = 1.23) compared to their counterparts in the baseline condition (M = 6.79; SD = 1.68; F(1, 246) = 5.26, p = .023). | A similar two-level (counterfactual comparison: nonsocial, social) between-subjects ANOVA on the attention measure revealed a significant main effect, such that participants in the social condition (M = .41, SD = 1.57) devoted more attention to the counterfactual alternative than did participants in the nonsocial condition (M = .79, SD = 1.52; F(1, 344) = 5.37, p = .02). | Feeling of Emptiness. As expected, a one-way (exclusion vs. inclusion) ANOVA showed that socially excluded participants reported a greater feeling of emptiness (M = 4.02, SD = 1.46) than their included counterparts (M = 2.73, SD = 1.24; F(1, 155) = 35.20; p < .001; n2 = .19). | We find that an increase in all hypothesized narrative elements significantly increases both narrative transportation (NT) and positive feedback (PF): landscape of affective consciousness (NT: b = .02, p < .001, R2 =.001; PF: b = .09, p < .001, R2 = .004), landscape of cognitive consciousness (NT: b = .03, p < .001, R2 = .002; PF: b = .03, p < .001, R2 = .001), spatial embedding (NT: b = .08, p < .001, R2 = .018; PF: b =.23, p < .001, R2 = .028), temporal embedding (NT: b = .07, p < .001, R2 = .008; PF: b =.17, p < .001, R2 = .011), comedies (NT: b = .13, p < .001, R2 = .039; PF: b = .51, p < .001, R2 = .061), tragedies (NT: b = .22, p < .001, R2 = .049; PF: b = .85, p < .001, R2 = .067), and early climax (drama; NT: b = .24, p < .001, R2 = .269; PF: b = .53, p < .001, R2 = .269). In summary, we find (further) support for hypotheses 1-6.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 260 columns across 12 data files.
#### Issues Identified

60 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 12 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: Noise in the process: Assessing the evidential value of mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology journals

text.text: Mediation analysis plays a central role in marketing research and consumer psychology by modeling the complex processes underlying total effects.

Like other inferential methods, tests of indirect effects are susceptible to false-positive results when multiple defensible analytic decisions can lead to different conclusions (i.e. researcher degrees of freedom).

To assess the collective evidential value of mediation analyses in marketing, we (1) measure the relative proximity (RP) of confidence intervals to zero and (2) aggregate a related set of RP scores into a single distribution.

Study 1 demonstrates how researcher degrees of freedom in mediation analysis, such as trying many different mediators and outcomes or testing moderated mediation, can inflate false-positive rates to up to 20% in the scenarios we examined.
This study also demonstrates the validity of the RP index by examining its correspondence with false-positive findings.
In Study 2, we compare the RP distribution of mediation analyses published in top marketing journals (2018-2020) to simulations of null effects, low power, and adequate power.
We find that mediation analyses in marketing substantially deviated from simulations with adequate power but were similar to simulated distributions with low power and null effects.
We propose study preregistration, increased statistical power, and reduction of selection bias as solutions to increase evidential value of mediation analyses going forward.
Keywords: mediation analysis, p-hacking, researcher degrees of freedom, moderated mediation, process analysis, indirect effect results.
Some mediation analyses may have been specified post hoc, although the analysis tools, like most inferential approaches, are designed to test preplanned hypotheses.

Pham and Oh (2021), argued that "most consumer research should probably be regarded as exploratory" (p. 168) and argued that, due to their complexity, we shouldn't expect mediation models to be specified a priori.
Adding further evidence that mediation analyses, as they are currently implemented, may not be truly confirmatory though they are customarily reported as such.

Janiszewski and van Osselaer (2021) provided survey data showing that only 25% of consumer research studies are purely deductive, meaning that exploration and post hoc testing play a role in the remaining 75% of studies.

Additionally, some methods papers actually advocate for testing many different mediation models to identify the "true mediator" (Fiedler, Harris, & Schott, 2018,   p. 96;Fiedler, Schott, & Meiser, 2011) or to find the true direction of causality (Wiedermann & von Eye, 2015).
text.formatted: Additionally, some methods papers actually advocate for testing many different mediation models to identify the "true mediator" (Fiedler, Harris, & Schott, 2018,   p. 96;<ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Fiedler, Schott, & Meiser, 2011)</ref> or to find the true direction of causality <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Wiedermann & von Eye, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These results cumulatively suggest that mediation analysis may be subject to selective reporting, which is when researchers share only certain findings or outcomes based on characteristics of the results (e.g., statistical significance, direction).
In this paper, we demonstrate how these practices can inflate false-positive error rates, which threatens the evidential value of the collective literature.
A literature or set of findings is said to have evidential value when selective reporting can be ruled out as the sole explanation for those findings (Simonsohn, et al. 2014).
text.formatted: A literature or set of findings is said to have evidential value when selective reporting can be ruled out as the sole explanation for those findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Simonsohn, et al. 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Misrepresentation of data exploration as confirmatory research and formal calls for systematic multiple testing may lead to inflated false-positive error rates through selective reporting, reducing evidential value.

This manuscript seeks to assess the evidential value of mediation analyses published in four high impact marketing and consumer psychology journals using a measure called relative proximity (RP;Götz et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This manuscript seeks to assess the evidential value of mediation analyses published in four high impact marketing and consumer psychology journals using a measure called relative proximity (RP;<ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Götz et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: RP has only been applied in one study (Götz et al., 2021), and

text.text: One of the core objectives of marketing research and consumer psychology is to go beyond an observable phenomenon and tap into the underlying processes (Holbrook & Batra, 1987; Sujan, 1985).
text.formatted: One of the core objectives of marketing research and consumer psychology is to go beyond an observable phenomenon and tap into the underlying processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Holbrook & Batra, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Sujan, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: Behavioral interventions, for instance, often affect choices through cognitive processes.

Mediation analysis allows researchers to test the consistency of observed data with hypothesized causal mechanisms and estimate the extent to which the total effect of a manipulation on an outcome variable is explained by a proposed mechanism, a mediator.
The generated insights are relevant for marketing and consumer psychology researchers for both theory testing and application.

For example, Li, Yin, and Xu (2026) found that in fundraising, when total goal amount (e.g., $6,400) is divisible by individual contribution request (e.g., $8), individuals are more likely to contribute, and that this effect is mediated by perceived clarity of the individual's contribution.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Li, Yin, and Xu (2026)</ref> found that in fundraising, when total goal amount (e.g., $6,400) is divisible by individual contribution request (e.g., $8), individuals are more likely to contribute, and that this effect is mediated by perceived clarity of the individual's contribution.

text.text: Their model applies theory from research on numerical cognition and collective goals, but it also identifies a practical mechanism by which other approaches to increasing donations could operate.
Mediation analysis has thus been increasingly used to deepen the understanding of the observed phenomena and heighten the relevance of the research.
A review of papers in the Journal of Consumer Research in 2014-2016 found 71% of articles with experiments included a mediation analysis (Pieters, 2017).
text.formatted: A review of papers in the Journal of Consumer Research in 2014-2016 found 71% of articles with experiments included a mediation analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Pieters, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In our own analysis, about half (47%) of all articles published in major marketing and consumer psychology journals contain a mediation analysis.
This enormous popularity is at least partially driven by the accessibility of software to estimate and conduct inference on indirect effects (e.g., the PROCESS macro, Hayes, 2022).
text.formatted: This enormous popularity is at least partially driven by the accessibility of software to estimate and conduct inference on indirect effects (e.g., the PROCESS macro, <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Hayes, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: There is however reason to believe that mediation analysis is not always conducted in a completely a priori manner, which has serious consequences for the validity of the reported has only been used to examine mediation analyses.

It was developed to evaluate evidential value from sets of statistical tests which primarily use confidence intervals (rather than p-values), and this measure requires additional validation, which we provide in Study 1.

Study 1 uses a Monte Carlo simulation study to demonstrate how flexibility in mediation analysis can manifest in false-positive rates far greater than the nominal 𝛼𝛼 level and this inflated false-positive rate is reflected accurately by the RP index.
Study 2 compares the distribution of published mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology with simulations of mediation analyses at different levels of statistical power.

Our results indicate that mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology research are typically underpowered and/or show signs of selective reporting, which substantially limits the evidential value of the literature.
We conclude by discussing ways to improve the evidential value of mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology research.

As most commonly used in consumer psychology and marketing research, a mediation analysis is a regression-based statistical model used to assess whether a proposed mediator (M) could be part of a causal chain between X and Y, such that X affects M which then affects Y (See Figure 1).

text.text: For example, Shaddy and colleagues (2026) found that consumers showed lower support of brands (Y) that used demographic targeting of advertisements (as compared to broad advertisements; X), and that this effect was mediated by appraisals of discrimination (M).

text.text: Mediation analysis is appealing because it can broaden the field's theoretical understanding of the effect itself by exploring why or how an effect occurs.
Additionally, identification of mediators provides greater opportunity to capitalize on this mechanism through other antecedent variables. through M.
Importantly, mediation analysis only analyzes covariance and does not provide evidence for causality.
Causality must be established through experimental design and theory (Hayes, 2022; Imai, Tingley, Yamamoto, 2013; Pieters, 2017; Rohrer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Causality must be established through experimental design and theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hayes, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Imai, Tingley, Yamamoto, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Pieters, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Rohrer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Caution is required when interpreting mediation results to clarify the distinction between results being consistent with a proposed causal model compared to evidence for the causal model itself.

Apart from a false-positive result, a significant indirect effect can also be the result of response style bias that affects the involved variables (e.g., acquiescence, midpoint responding; Baumgartner and Steenkamp 2001), "meaningless mediation" where M is really a different measure of Y or a manipulation check (Lynch, 2011; Zhao, Lynch, & Chen 2010), demand effects, confounds, or other problems (MacKinnon et al., 2000).
text.formatted: Apart from a false-positive result, a significant indirect effect can also be the result of response style bias that affects the involved variables (e.g., acquiescence, midpoint responding; <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Baumgartner and Steenkamp 2001)</ref>, "meaningless mediation" where M is really a different measure of Y or a manipulation check <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Lynch, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Zhao, Lynch, & Chen 2010)</ref>, demand effects, confounds, or other problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(MacKinnon et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers using mediation analysis have frequently been critiqued for generating causal claims that are unfounded, underreporting causal identification assumptions which clarify issues around confounding and temporal ordering (Imai et al., 2010; Tate, 2015; Vo et al., 2020).

text.text: While confounding can bias a point estimate, even in causal mediation approaches that attempt to address these biases, confidence interval approaches are used for making statistical inference.

Even the absence of confounding biases and perfect application of causal inference approaches (which primarily are about textual interpretations and assumption transparency), would not remove the issue this manuscript focuses on: bias in reporting and conduct of mediation analysis based on preference for statistically significant effects.

A few marketing scholars have ably argued for a more colorful palette of epistemological and methodological approaches to marketing and consumer psychology research exploring mechanisms (Inman et al., 2018; Lynch et al., 2012; Pham, 2013; Peracchio, Luce, & McGill, 2014).

text.text: But mediation analysis continues to play a prominent role in many leading marketing and consumer psychology journals (Pieters, 2017).

text.text: This is true of experimental consumer psychology, but also of other adjacent sub-fields of marketing.

This powerful push for process evidence has even spilled over into consumer culture theory, where researchers increasingly use qualitative methods to understand consumer processes (e.g., "hegemonic memory making" Brunk, Giesler, & Hartmann, 2017; Giesler & Thompson, 2016).
text.formatted: This powerful push for process evidence has even spilled over into consumer culture theory, where researchers increasingly use qualitative methods to understand consumer processes (e.g., "hegemonic memory making" <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Brunk, Giesler, & Hartmann, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Giesler & Thompson, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, with the few exceptions of modeling and quantitative review papers, one is hard-pressed to find empirical papers that lack mediation analyses.
In our own review, we found that of 647 papers in the top four marketing and consumer psychology journals in 2018 -2020, 308 (47.6%) contained at least one mediation analysis.

Statistical inference for the indirect effect of X on Y through M is different from other standard approaches since the indirect effect is the product of the estimated effects of X on M (𝑎𝑎) and M on Y controlling for X (𝑎𝑎).
The indirect effect has an unusual sampling distribution, where the shape and spread is dependent on the population values of the a and b paths separately.

Null hypothesis significance testing is difficult in the context of mediation because there is no single null distribution for the indirect effect (Tofighi, 2020), thus reporting p-values for tests of mediation is relatively rare.
text.formatted: Null hypothesis significance testing is difficult in the context of mediation because there is no single null distribution for the indirect effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Tofighi, 2020)</ref>, thus reporting p-values for tests of mediation is relatively rare.

text.text: As a consequence, the indirect effect (𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎) is typically reported with a confidence interval (CI).
There exist many different methods to generate the confidence interval around an indirect effect.

Currently, bootstrap confidence intervals for the indirect effect, as proposed by Shrout and Bolger (2002), are the preferred method of inference with the most common tool being the PROCESS macro (Hayes, 2022).
text.formatted: Currently, bootstrap confidence intervals for the indirect effect, as proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Shrout and Bolger (2002)</ref>, are the preferred method of inference with the most common tool being the PROCESS macro <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hayes, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Bootstrapping methods outperform methods that assume a normal sampling distribution by having higher statistical power and more appropriate false-positive error rates (Biesanz, Falk, & Savalei, 2010; Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007; MacKinnon, Lockwood, & Williams, 2004).
text.formatted: Bootstrapping methods outperform methods that assume a normal sampling distribution by having higher statistical power and more appropriate false-positive error rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Biesanz, Falk, & Savalei, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">MacKinnon, Lockwood, & Williams, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The CI can be used to determine statistical significance: Consider for example, a 95% CI of [0.01, 0.03].
In this example the coefficient is deemed statistically significant at 𝛼𝛼 = .05 level, because the 95% CI does not include zero.
But, from this interval, we cannot tell if the coefficient is significant at 𝛼𝛼 = 0.01.
This leaves a gap between what could be known with a pvalue compared to a bootstrap CI, because readers cannot know whether an effect would be significant at any level other than what is reported.
This issue is somewhat unique to bootstrap CIs, as with parametric CIs it is typically possible to back-calculate the standard error and generate all possible CIs or p-values.

Preregistering, or preplanning a mediation analysis may pose difficulties to some researchers, since it requires a deeper understanding of the structure of the data compared to preregistering the hypotheses and procedures for testing a total effect.
But deciding on the analysis post hoc increases the risk that decisions are guided by potentially random patterns in the data (Nosek, Ebersole, DeHaven, & Mellor, 2018).
text.formatted: But deciding on the analysis post hoc increases the risk that decisions are guided by potentially random patterns in the data <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Nosek, Ebersole, DeHaven, & Mellor, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: When comparing dissertations to publications in management research, researchers often add/drop data, covariates, and hypotheses before publishing in peer-reviewed journals (Kepes et al., 2022).
text.formatted: When comparing dissertations to publications in management research, researchers often add/drop data, covariates, and hypotheses before publishing in peer-reviewed journals <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Kepes et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This problem, well known from other analyses, is aggravated in the case of mediation analyses since the analyses allow for a large number of configurations that offer many researcher degrees of freedom (Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn, 2011).
text.formatted: This problem, well known from other analyses, is aggravated in the case of mediation analyses since the analyses allow for a large number of configurations that offer many researcher degrees of freedom <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, while replication studies are increasingly conducted in marketing and consumer psychology to add evidential value for an established effect, replications typically focus on total effects instead of indirect effects.
Given the prominence and relevance of mediation analyses in marketing it is important to evaluate the evidential value using the information that is reported in mediation analyses.

The lack of p-values-specifically the lack of a standard approach for calculating the p-value of indirect effects-constrains the application of existing methods that have been developed to assess the evidential value in a set of empirical findings (e.g., Simonsohn et al. 2014; but see Morey & Davis-Stober, 2026).

text.text: To that goal we refer to a more recently developed method that estimates evidential value based on the ratio of a CI's distance to zero and the width of the CI (Götz et al., 2021).
text.formatted: To that goal we refer to a more recently developed method that estimates evidential value based on the ratio of a CI's distance to zero and the width of the CI <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Götz et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The distance, the ratio's numerator, is a function of the size of the effect, while the width of the CI, the denominator, indicates uncertainty in the estimate.
Thus, larger ratios indicate stronger evidence.
Following this reasoning, Götz and colleagues (2021) call this ratio the "relative proximity" of the CI to zero (RP).
text.formatted: Following this reasoning, <ref type="bibr">Götz and colleagues (2021)</ref> call this ratio the "relative proximity" of the CI to zero (RP).

text.text: If CIs are systematically too close to zero it is indicative of low evidential value like what is signaled by p-values that are systematically too close to .05.
Thus, when applied to mediation analysis this test statistic divides the distance to zero of an indirect effect's CI by the range of the CI.

RP can be mathematically represented as a function of the upper bound of the CI (𝐶𝐶𝐼𝐼 𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢 ) and the lower bound of the CI (𝐶𝐶𝐼𝐼 𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢 ), where the 𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠 function indicates the mathematical sign of a number:

This equation breaks down the distance of the CI from zero, min��𝐶𝐶𝐼𝐼 𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢 �, |𝐶𝐶𝐼𝐼 𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢 |�, whether it is positive or negative, and scales by the width of the CI, 𝐶𝐶𝐼𝐼 𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢 -𝐶𝐶𝐼𝐼 𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑙𝑢𝑢𝑢𝑢 .

This value is then multiplied by +1 if both the upper and lower bounds have the same sign (i.e., the interval does not include zero), as their product will be positive, or -1 if the upper and lower bounds have different signs (i.e., the interval does include zero), as their product will be negativefoot_0 .

The interval is 3 CI widths away from zero.
Whereas for an interval [-2,4], the minimum distance is 2, width is 6, and sign of the product is -1, so the 𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅 = 2 6 × -1 = -.33.

The RP is somewhat more difficult to interpret when it's negative, but it is useful to note that when a CI is symmetric around zero (e.g., [-2,2]) the RP will be equal to -0.5, which is its minimum possible value.

text.text: A positive RP indicates a CI that excludes zero and is thus statistically significant, whereas a negative RP indicates a CI that overlaps with zero and is not statistically significant.
As CIs move further from zero and/or become narrower due to greater precision, RPs grow larger, a phenomenon comparable to the increasing t or z statistics as statistical power improves.
Even a true effect can result in an RP score that is very close to zero due to random chance.
However, the likelihood that this occurs across many studies is very low.

So, while a single study with a low RP cannot be used to identify a false-positive result, we can aggregate a set of RP scores together to see if there is a pattern of RP scores that are too close to zero, which would indicate a lack of evidential value (Adler, Roseler, & Schoniger, 2023).

text.text: Additionally, they demonstrated that the RP distributions across five psychology journals show evidence of selection bias, meaning low evidential value.
In our study we focus on validating the RP measure through additional simulation studies and using RP to evaluate published mediation analyses from top marketing and consumer psychology journals.
Study 1 demonstrates the effect of specific researcher degrees of freedom on both false-positive rates and RP.

These results build on Götz and colleagues (2021) by demonstrating the correspondence between RP and false positives as well as examining which specific practices in mediation analyses have the greatest impact on evidential value.

text.text: In Study 2, we extract RP values from published mediation analysis in four top marketing and consumer psychology journals, comparing the distribution to simulated values to evaluate existing evidential value of mediation results in marketing and consumer psychology.
The purpose of Study 1 is to explore the impact of analytical flexibility (i.e., researcher degrees of freedom) on the false-positive error rates and RP distributions of indirect tests.
We simulated analytical flexibilities that are specific to mediation analysis to evaluate how each practice impacts the false-positive error rate and RP distribution.
In their seminal paper, Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011) introduced the field of psychology to the concept of researcher degrees of freedom (RDFs).
text.formatted: In their seminal paper, <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011)</ref> introduced the field of psychology to the concept of researcher degrees of freedom (RDFs).

text.text: The authors used Monte Carlo simulations to demonstrate how flexibility in choice of the outcome variable, sample size, covariates, and conditions (as well as the combination of these practices) inflate false-positive error rates.
The original authors focused on main effects in a two-condition design, and their results emphasized how common practices in the field lead to surprisingly high false-positive error rates.
Researchers practicing in marketing and psychology need to consider similar issues with currently common practices in mediation analysis.
Our focus in this simulation are RDFs which are specific to mediation analysis and especially those that have been advocated by researchers in the field.

Specifically, we consider swapping the role of variables in the analysis (mediators and outcomes), choosing among candidate mediators and outcomes, testing moderation of different paths in the mediation analysis, including or excluding a covariate, trying multiple inferential methods for testing the indirect effect, and rerunning resampling procedures.
We examine two primary outcomes: false-positive error rate and distribution of the RP index.
We assume that RDFs have consequences of different severity on these indicators.
We simulate data under varied null hypotheses, where either the a-path or the b-path is zero and the other path varies in its magnitude.
The direct effect is fixed at 0 throughout the simulationsfoot_1 .
text.formatted: The direct effect is fixed at 0 throughout the simulations<ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">foot_1</ref> .

text.text: Sample size is fixed to 224, which was the median sample size in the studies examined in Study 2.
In each condition, 2,000 simulations are run, and when resampling/bootstrapping procedures are used they have 1,000 resamples.
We expected that under the null-hypothesis, each RDF will increase false-positive error rate and result in a higher RP index distribution.

Among the different RDFs, we expect multiple inferential methods and rerunning bootstraps to have the smallest effects on false-positive error rates (i.e., they are relatively ineffective methods for p-hacking).

Based on Hayes and Scharkow's (2013) agreement among inferential methods tends to be relatively high, and so we expect trying multiple inferential methods will not affect false-positive error rates very much.
text.formatted: Based on <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Hayes and Scharkow's (2013)</ref> agreement among inferential methods tends to be relatively high, and so we expect trying multiple inferential methods will not affect false-positive error rates very much.

text.text: Similarly, bootstrap confidence intervals should be relatively stable with 1,000 resamples, so repeating them is unlikely to result in a large inflation of false-positive errors.
By contrast we hypothesized that choosing among candidate mediators and outcomes and testing moderation will result in the highest false-positive error rates.
These two decisions increase the number of available tests the most, presenting the greatest opportunity for inflated false-positive error rates.

In this section we summarize the results of the simulation study, discussing first the results for false positives then the results for RP distribution.
Overall the simulation shows that the explored RDFs do indeed increase false-positive error rates, and differentially so across practices.
The distribution of RP is similarly perturbed in line with the patterns of false positives.

text.text: First examining the no RDF condition, false-positive error rates are well controlled and close to .05 when the non-zero path is sufficiently large, and somewhat conservative (less than .05) when the non-zero path is small.
This result is in line with many prior simulations in mediation analysis (Hayes & Scharkow, 2013; Biesanz et al., 2010; MacKinnon et al., 2004).
text.formatted: This result is in line with many prior simulations in mediation analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Hayes & Scharkow, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Biesanz et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">MacKinnon et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The most innocuous RDF was covariate inclusion/exclusion (False-positive rate range .0265 -.0555).
False positives were not particularly inflated under this method, though it was always greater than the no researcher degree of freedom condition.
Notably, the covariate was generated to be independent of all of the other variables in the model, to be consistent with the idea that this variable is unnecessary.
Whereas, if the covariate was correlated with the variables in the model, it could be viewed as a confounder, and then should be included in the model.
The choice to keep the covariate independent, may have resulted in very limited impact on falsepositive rate.
Results may differ with covariates which are correlated with other variables in the mediation model.
Multiple inferential methods and rerunning bootstraps had a non-trivial but generally small effect on false-positive error rates (.0530 -.0705 and .0365 -.0805, respectively).
Similarly, swapping M and Y has a somewhat small effect (.0250 -.0900), yet it was notable that this seemed to have more of an effect when the a-path was zero compared to when the b-path was zero.
When the b-path is nonzero, swapping M and Y maintains that relationship on the bpath while giving a "second chance" to the a-path.
Whereas when the b-path is zero, swapping M and Y result in minimal change in the results.

There were a few approaches that inflated false-positive error rates to unacceptable levels: choices of M and Y (.0455 -.1940) and testing moderated mediation with either the index of moderated mediation (.0515 -.1480) or the conditional indirect effects (.0755 -.2040).
Notably, both of these estimates could be underestimating the impact these options have in real research.
In real research, researchers could test more variables, leading to even higher error rates.
We only allowed for two options for M and two options for Y whereas real research may have many more options.
Similarly, for moderated mediation we only looked at one possible moderator.
In practice, these false-positive error rates could be much higher.

Overall our hypotheses were confirmed: rerunning bootstraps, inferential methods, and covariates were the least impactful practices; whereas, choices of variables and moderated mediation inflate false-positive error rates the most.

While these results shed light on the potential impact of these research practices on the evidential value of mediation analysis, they can also provide additional support for the validity of the RP index, which is a relatively new statistic.
We can assess how these RDFs impact the distribution of the RP and whether the results are aligned with those seen for false positives.

If the outcomes are aligned this suggests that RP can operate as a valid proxy for examining false positives within contexts very closely aligned to those in the simulation (i.e., specific to mediation analysis).

text.text: The primary features of this graph show that the RDFs that most strongly impacted false positives (Choice of M and Y and Moderated Mediation) shift the RP distribution right relative to the no RDF distributions.
For the practices that impacted false positives least (covariates, inferential method, and rerunning bootstraps) the distributions look most similar to the no RDF condition.
Just as was seen with the false positives, the difference between RP distributions when a is nonzero vs. when b is nonzero, mirrors the differences we observed with false-positive rates.
Overall, this demonstrates that when RDFs are utilized, this will manifest in the distribution of the RP, specifically in a shift of the distribution right, toward more positive values.

Study 1 is a Monte Carlo simulation that demonstrates how different RDFs can impact false positives and relative proximity in mediation analysis.

Overall, we find very close correspondence between the RP and false positives, suggesting the RP may serve as a reliable index by which to evaluate the evidential value of published mediation literature.
Notably, RP has not been evaluated for contexts outside of mediation.
Additionally, we identified specific practices which have a large impact on false-positive rates: choice of mediators and outcomes and testing moderated mediation.
These practices suggest that preregistration of mediation (and moderated mediation) analysis is recommended to provide transparency about whether specific mediation models were hypothesized a priori.

Study 2: Comparing Marketing and Consumer Psychology Journals to Simulated

The purpose of Study 2 was to test how RP scores calculated from mediation analyses reported in marketing and consumer psychology journals compared to data simulated under a variety of population conditions.
To this end, we simulated three different RP distributions (low power, adequate power, and null effects).
The simulated distributions were separately plotted against the marketing and consumer psychology journal distribution so that we could examine the similarity among the four distributions.
In this way, we hoped to examine whether the observed data showed the most similarity to adequately powered tests, low-powered tests, null tests, or a mixture of these categories.
Our first step in comparing RP distributions was to collect reported CIs from marketing and consumer psychology journals and convert them to RP scores.

The data were compiled from four highly cited marketing and consumer psychology journals, the Journal of Consumer Psychology, the Journal of Consumer Research, the Journal of Marketing and the Journal of Marketing Research during a three-year period (2018-20) 4 .

text.text: Next, we simulated mediation analyses that were adequately powered (80-95% power), low-powered (33-79% power) and null effects (~5% false-positive rate).
We then compared the distribution of RP scores from the mediation analyses to the simulated distributions.

Additionally, we describe how we simulated data to evaluate alignment of RP distributions.
Finally, we describe how we compared the observed RP distributions to the simulated distributions.

text.text: To test the collective evidential value of mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology journals, we conducted a systematic review of reported test statistics.
We chose the following high impact journals for our analysis: Journal of Consumer Research (JCR), and
Research (JMR).
We selected these journals because they have high impact factors and represent typical outlets for mediation studies in marketing.
We analyzed three years of each of the preceding journals, which covered all articles which appeared in print between 2018 and 2020 for each journal.
Our initial sample contained 647 publications.

Using keywords such as mediation, indirect, Hayes, and PROCESS, a laboratory assistant and the fourth author manually reviewed each article to identify those containing at least one mediation model with accompanying CI.
This initial screening of publications resulted in a sample of 308 publications.

During analysis, we excluded and additional 13 publications which contained multilevel models (6), were repeated-measures designs (2), were retracted (2), were non-linear mediation models (1), or were in retrospect found not to contain any mediation model ( 2).
text.formatted: During analysis, we excluded and additional 13 publications which contained multilevel models (6), were repeated-measures designs (2), were retracted (2), were non-linear mediation models (1), or were in retrospect found not to contain any mediation model ( <ref type="formula" target="#formula_1">2</ref>).

text.text: An additional ten papers were unusable because they lacked a codable CI.
This process resulted in a final dataset of 285 mediation analyses.
The articles that included mediation were then given to a team of six laboratory assistants who were trained to manually code mediation analyses, but naive to the hypotheses.

We chose to apply manual harvesting of test statistics rather than mechanical harvesting because research articles tend to include many test statistics that are not central to the core hypotheses and therefore less informative regarding problems with evidence quality (Simonsohn et al., 2014).
text.formatted: We chose to apply manual harvesting of test statistics rather than mechanical harvesting because research articles tend to include many test statistics that are not central to the core hypotheses and therefore less informative regarding problems with evidence quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Simonsohn et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Working independently, pairs of assistants were instructed to record the first reported hypothesized test of an indirect effect mentioned in the publication subject to two exceptions.
If the first reported test was to rule out alternative explanations, the assistants were told to ignore these tests in favor of tests which were hypothesized.
In the case of moderated mediation, the assistants were told to record the index of moderated mediation, if it was reported, even if it was not reported before any other indirect effects.

The selected articles were manually coded, to record the first reported hypothesized test of an indirect effect mentioned in the publication, the hypothesis test, the point estimates of the indirect effect or the index of moderated mediation, its standard error and/or the CIs around the point estimate, as well as the formal hypothesis on which the test was based.

If reported, further details about the component paths in the mediation model, such as point estimates, effect sizes (group means and standard deviations), or inferential statistics (F-test or t-test) were recorded along with other details about the estimation (the confidence level of the interval, the model number of the PROCESS macro used, and what kind of interval was calculated, and using how many bootstrap samples).

text.text: To simulate the adequate and low powered true effects, we used a weak population-level indirect effect (ab=.04) and a residual direct effect of zero.

We selected ab=.04 because it allowed us to achieve desired power levels using sample sizes that are similar to those reported in marketing and consumer psychology journals and is in-line with previous meta-analyses of mediation (Götz et al., 2021; Aberson, 2019b).

text.text: We considered three possible population models: the X-M correlation is equal to the M-Y correlation (rXM = .20, rMY = .20, rXY = .04), the X-M correlation is four times the size of the M-Y correlation (rXM = .4, rMY = .1, rXY = .04), and the X-M correlation is one quarter of the M-Y correlation (rXM = .1, rMY = .4, rXY = .04).
The means and standard deviations of X, M, and Y were always 0 and 1, respectively.
We manipulated power by varying the sample size of each simulated data set while holding all other parameters constant.

text.text: For null effects, we ran simple mediation analyses on a series of simulated 3-variable data sets in which all population correlations among variables was set to zero except one path (apath or b-path), which was assigned to have weak (.1), moderate (.3), strong (.5; Cohen, 1988), or very strong correlations (.7).

text.text: The discontinuity of the distribution at zero also provides clear evidence for selection bias, whereby results with CIs including zero are not published at the same rate as would be expected under any of these distributions.
Although mediation analysis has been regularly criticized for being underpowered (Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007), nearly all observed results were statistically significant.

text.text: This means that either effect sizes for indirect effects are much larger than anticipated, or selective reporting is biasing the observed literature.

Indeed, the observed distribution of RP scores is highly suggestive of some form of selection bias: Even with good (80-95%) statistical power, some portion of tests should result in false negative (5-20%), yielding negative RP scores.
Very few negative RP scores were observed in the literature, suggesting high statistical power cannot be the only explanation for these results.
This paper demonstrates the utility of the RP index for assessing the evidential value of mediation analysis through both simulation and empirical demonstration.

The first simulation demonstrates that the RP index corresponds closely to false-positive rates and using this tool we can identify analysis practices in mediation which can result in high false-positive rates.
Specifically, choosing among many candidate mediators and outcomes as well as testing moderated mediation, can increase false-positive rates to up to 20%.
Notably, both practices could be identified, or even avoided, if preregistration was more common for mediation analyses in marketing and consumer psychology.
Given the centrality of mediation analysis to theory building in consumer research, using preregistration for mediation analysis is of particular importance.
The second study focused on issues of power by comparing simulated data to empirical data using the RP index.
We find that the empirical data is discernibly different from high power but is also not completely consistent with low power or false positives.
This suggests that the empirical distribution may be a mixture of low power and false-positive results.

These results are particularly important in combination with the simulation results of Study 1 because it suggests that common practices which inflate the false-positive rate could result in a distribution like the observed one; however, it is not possible to differentiate between low power and researcher degrees of freedom using the RP index.

We propose three potential solutions to improve the evidential value of confirmatory mediation analyses: (1) preregistration, (2) designing adequately powered studies, and (3) reducing selection bias.
Preregistration creates documentary evidence that confirmatory analyses were indeed planned prior to seeing the data and making deviations away from planned analyses transparent.
When initial analyses do not support hypotheses, some researchers may be tempted to engage in questionable research practice (e.g., p-hacking).
Many adjacent fields, particularly within psychology, have adopted the practice of preregistration to make p-hacking more transparent.
Simmons and colleagues (2021) argued that preregistration promotes accurate reporting of confirmatory tests while still allowing for data exploration, if exploration is noted as such.

Preregistration can also be used when replicating an exploratory analysis to ensure the findings are consistent across independent samples, this can be particularly useful in cases with complex analytical pipelines that are difficult to specify in advance.
An exploratory approach can be taken with one sample to determine the analysis pipeline, then that pipeline is replicated in a confirmatory sample.
Calls for mediation analyses to be preregistered have been increasing in recent years (Montoya, 2024; Arch, Fishbein, Finkelstein, & Luoma, 2024; Keener, Kepes, & Torka, 2023; Torka et al., 2023).

text.text: A specific and precise preregistration of a mediation analysis should specify each analysis choice explored as an RDF in Study 1.
It should clearly specify the variables, how they are measured, and their roles in the mediation analysis, including moderators and covariates.
If moderators are hypothesized, the preregistration should specify which paths are hypothesized to be moderated and if using PROCESS which model number will be used.

Which inferential method will be used for the indirect effect should be specified in advance, and those using bootstrapping or resampling procedures can even preregister the number of resamples and the seed number.
For more recommendations on preregistering mediation analyses see Montoya (2024).

text.text: The observed RP distribution was not consistent with high statistical power, meaning that low statistical power is one possible explanation for the RP distribution of mediation analyses published in marketing and consumer psychology research.
This means that the sample sizes, the effect sizes, or both are too small to reliably detect true indirect effects when they exist.

Although sample sizes in marketing have increased in recent years with the availability of online samples, average effect sizes have decreased, leaving average power largely unchanged (Krefeld-Schwalb & Scheibehenne, 2023).
text.formatted: Although sample sizes in marketing have increased in recent years with the availability of online samples, average effect sizes have decreased, leaving average power largely unchanged <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Krefeld-Schwalb & Scheibehenne, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Mediation analyses may require larger sample sizes than currently used.
Meta-analytic evidence suggests that the average indirect effect is around 0.07 standardized units, which is less than half of what is typically considered small (Götz et al., 2021; Aberson, 2019b).

text.text: For example, a simple mediation analysis that involves one small (d = 0.2) standardized effect (a weak relationship between mediator and either predictor or outcome variable) requires a sample size of N = 385 to have 80% power (Fritz & MacKinnon, 2007).

text.text: Researchers should consider both their tests of total effects and mediation analyses when planning sample size, as these two tests do not often have the same level of power (Kenny & Judd, 2014; Giner-Sorolla et al., 2018).

text.text: Available tools can help determine the sample size necessary to obtain desired statistical power to detect and indirect effect given information about what the strength of relationship among the various variables may be (Schoemann et al. 2017; Aberson, 2019a).

text.text: Either increasing sample size, studying larger effect sizes, or both can increase statistical power to detect indirect effects.
Another area where power can be improved is through improved measurement and measurement modeling.
Selecting measurement instruments with better reliability can improve statistical power to detect effects (Williams & Zimmerman, 1989; Leon, Marzuk, & Portera, 1995).

text.text: This can often mean using longer scales with more informative items or selecting scales that have been vetted in previous research rather than designing your own scale for the specific study (Flake, Pek, & Hehman 2017).
text.formatted: This can often mean using longer scales with more informative items or selecting scales that have been vetted in previous research rather than designing your own scale for the specific study <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Flake, Pek, & Hehman 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Latent variable modeling can be used to account for measurement error and improve power to detect indirect effects (Sim, Kim, & Suh 2021).

text.text: In many of the studies included in this analysis either the outcome variable or the mediator could have easily been incorporated as a latent variable, and perhaps power would be improved.

Alternatively, errors-in-measurement approaches have recently been incorporated to the PROCESS macro, which allow for accounting for the reliability of a scale and can also increase statistical power (Hayes, Allison, & Alexander, 2025).

text.text: The RP distribution indicates the presence of selection bias based on mediation analyses, which is a novel finding given that these analyses are not typically the "primary" analyses.
Selection bias can manifest at a variety of stages of research, where researchers may choose not to submit, editors may desk reject, or reviewers may negatively review, non-significant results.
Typically, when the source is a part of the peer review process, this is called publication bias, but all of these behaviors manifest as selection bias.

Selection bias is problematic because it inflates effect size estimates in meta-analysis (Friese & Frankenbach, 2020), reduces the number of true negatives in the published literature (Bakker, van Dijk, & Wicherts, 2012), and incentivizes researchers to "find" significant results because they cannot publish otherwise.
text.formatted: Selection bias is problematic because it inflates effect size estimates in meta-analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Friese & Frankenbach, 2020)</ref>, reduces the number of true negatives in the published literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bakker, van Dijk, & Wicherts, 2012)</ref>, and incentivizes researchers to "find" significant results because they cannot publish otherwise.

text.text: Previous research on publication bias has focused on how the results of primary hypothesis tests can influence likelihood of publication, but the current research shows that even mediation analyses (which are typically secondary) also show strong evidence of selection bias.
To reduce selection bias authors, reviewers, and editors need to be open to publishing meaningful and interesting null results.
Statistical methods such as equivalence testing can help quantify the evidentiary value of failures to reject the null hypothesis (Lakens et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Statistical methods such as equivalence testing can help quantify the evidentiary value of failures to reject the null hypothesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Lakens et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Registered reports implement a twostage peer review process, where the study is reviewed after the study is planned, but before data is collected/analyzed.

After peer review the manuscript is given an "in-principle acceptance" which means that it will be published regardless of the results, which should reduce publication bias immensely (Chambers, 2013).
text.formatted: After peer review the manuscript is given an "in-principle acceptance" which means that it will be published regardless of the results, which should reduce publication bias immensely <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chambers, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence suggests that about 56% of registered reports include null results as compared to 4% of traditional publications (Scheel, Schijen, & Lakens, 2021).
text.formatted: Evidence suggests that about 56% of registered reports include null results as compared to 4% of traditional publications <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Scheel, Schijen, & Lakens, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Registered reports have yet to be adopted by marketing and consumer psychology journals (Montoya, Krenzer, & Fossum, 2021), and so one way to reduce publication bias in this field would be implementing this new publication mechanism at top journals in this field.
text.formatted: Registered reports have yet to be adopted by marketing and consumer psychology journals <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Montoya, Krenzer, & Fossum, 2021)</ref>, and so one way to reduce publication bias in this field would be implementing this new publication mechanism at top journals in this field.

text.text: The problems of evidential value that we have uncovered in published marketing and consumer psychology studies should encourage authors, readers, reviewers and editors to exert caution in the future when evaluating process evidence.
Moreover, the possible causes we have identified-low power, selection bias, and p-hacking (even if unintentional)-are not unique to mediation analyses.
The same evidential value issues could be present in other statistical tests, even if not detectable through meta-analyses.
This research should help bring more emphasis to study preregistration and methods of increasing statistical power to improve the validity of future mediation analyses.
Simulation studies necessarily lack much of the complexity and diversity of a set of realworld studies.
This is because (1) it is impossible to identify and quantify every force that influences data from actual studies, and (2) simulations that are too complex are uninterpretable.

For example, while the empirical results from the marketing and consumer psychology journals are a mix of simple mediation, multiple mediation, and moderated mediation, we only generated results from simple mediation models for the simulation.
We selected parameters that we hoped would most closely mimic what is reported in marketing and consumer psychology journals.
We have not been able to conceive of a scenario that would diminish the findings we have reported.
It is important to note that even RP distributions that perfectly match or exceed what we would expect from highly powered true results can mask severe defects.
The RP distribution only gives an indication of whether there is a substantial, obvious presence of false-positive results or underpowered studies.

The RP distribution gives no information about issues of causal order, confounds, lack of discriminant validity among modeled variables, and other issues that frequently arise and must be dealt with in inferential statistical tests such as mediation analyses (Rohrer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The RP distribution gives no information about issues of causal order, confounds, lack of discriminant validity among modeled variables, and other issues that frequently arise and must be dealt with in inferential statistical tests such as mediation analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Rohrer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The RP statistic is only recently proposed and has only been applied to evaluation of indirect effects (Götz et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The RP statistic is only recently proposed and has only been applied to evaluation of indirect effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Götz et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: RP has not been applied in other contexts, and its statistical properties are still understudied.

This issue was addressed in the current study by matching simulations to the applied examples, but this also introduces flexibilities that limit the use of RP as a general approach for evaluating evidential value.

As such, the application of RP to broader contexts should be conducted with caution, and methodological research on the general properties of the RP is needed before this method can be widely adopted and applied.

Recent criticisms of the other methods for evaluating evidential value (Morey & Davis-Stober, 2026), should give pause to researchers aiming to evaluate evidential value of a broad literature, as these methods were widely adopted prior to their statistical properties being evaluated.
text.formatted: Recent criticisms of the other methods for evaluating evidential value <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Morey & Davis-Stober, 2026)</ref>, should give pause to researchers aiming to evaluate evidential value of a broad literature, as these methods were widely adopted prior to their statistical properties being evaluated.

text.text: The same mistake should not be made with RP or test statistics derived from RP, and researchers interested in using RP should evaluate whether it performs accurately in a given context before being applied.

In aggregate, confidence intervals (CIs) reported for mediation analyses are sensitive to researcher degrees of freedom such as trying multiple mediators and testing many different moderated mediation models.
These practices lead to increased false positive rates and larger RP indices.
RP indices in marketing and consumer psychology journals do not match a pattern of adequately-powered results in data simulations.
The bulk of reported CIs are too close to zero relative to their widths (low RP scores).
This could reflect low power, null effects, and/or researcher degrees of freedom.
This result is problematic because mediation analyses play a central role in helping researchers to understand the process by which predictor variables influence outcomes of interest.
Thankfully, regardless of which situation is true (low power, null effects, or RDFs), all can be addressed in similar ways.
We suggest three primary solutions: study preregistration, increasing power, and reducing selection bias.
Another issue to consider is how to handle non-confirmatory research.
Conducting exploratory analyses and reporting them as confirmatory could be part of the.

If true, that would indicate that there is a need or at least an appetite for non-confirmatory, perhaps non-reductionist, approaches. Janiszewski and van Osselaer (2021) contribute to this area by showing how a combination of exploratory and confirmatory analyses could be reported.
